name: Kingdom of Cambodia (after Angkor)
summary: Cambodia after the court left Angkor in 1431: a smaller Khmer kingdom with capitals near Phnom Penh, squeezed between Siam and Vietnam, which became a French protectorate in 1863.

location.value: Mainland Southeast Asia, in territory that is now Cambodia, Vietnam and Thailand; the capital moved from Chaktomuk (1431–1525) to Longvek (1525–1594), Srey Sarchor, and Oudong (1620–1863).

terrain.value: Wide floodplains around the Tonlé Sap and the Mekong, which flood every rainy season.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon: a wet season from May to October and a hot dry season.

resources.value: Rice, rich fisheries in the Tonlé Sap, and forest goods such as deerskins, lacquer and ivory.

disasters.value: Floods, droughts and the destruction caused by repeated invasions.

urbanisation.value: Royal capitals at Srei Santhor, Longvek (1500s) and Oudong (from about 1618), and the trading town of Phnom Penh.

migration.value: Vietnamese settlers in the Mekong delta.

economicBase.value: Trade was essential: precious stones, metals, silk, cotton, ivory, livestock and rhinoceros horn. Rice and fishing are not covered in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: Mekong trade with Chinese and European merchants.

wealth.value: Modest; trade at Phnom Penh brought some wealth to the court.

moneyAndTax.value: Taxes paid in rice and labour; King Ang Duong issued Cambodia’s first modern coins (1847).

inequality.value: The king and royal family, officials and monks above peasant farmers and slaves.

governmentType.value: A monarchy; Siam captured Longvek in 1594, Vietnam ruled from 1834 to 1847, and the kingdom lost its sovereignty under joint suzerainty until the French protectorate was signed by Norodom on 11 August 1863.

keyRulers.value: Ponhea Yat (from 1431), Ang Chan I (1516–1566, moved the capital to Longvek), Ang Duong (the page gives 1848–1860, not 1841) and Norodom. In 1642 King Ponhea Chan converted to Islam and reigned as Ramathipadi I.

succession.value: Royal family; disputes invited foreign help.

institutions.value: The royal court, provincial governors and the Buddhist monkhood (sangha).

stability.value: Siam and Vietnam alternately demanded tribute; from the 17th century Cambodia gradually lost control of the Mekong Delta.

eliteConflict.value: Princes backed by Siam fought princes backed by Vietnam for the throne.

armyAndTech.value: War elephants, infantry and war canoes on the rivers; some firearms from European traders.

majorWars.value: Siamese forces captured and sacked Longvek in 1594.

territoryChange.value: Lost the Mekong delta to Vietnam (1600s–1700s).

alliancesRivals.value: Caught between Siam and Vietnam; Portuguese, Spanish and Dutch adventurers and traders also intervened.

scienceEducation.value: Monastery schools taught boys reading, Buddhist texts and the Chbap moral verses.

openness.value: Open to Chinese, Malay, Japanese and European traders at Phnom Penh.

communicationTransport.value: Rivers and the Tonlé Sap lake were the main highways; ox-carts on land.

religion.value: Theravada Buddhism (adopted as state religion under Indravarman III, c. 1295–1308); Ponhea Chan became a Muslim in 1642. Angkor Wat as a pilgrimage site is not covered in the part of the page read.

languageWriting.value: Middle Khmer, written in Khmer script; literature such as the Reamker (the Khmer Ramayana).

artsArchitecture.value: Wooden Buddhist temples and palaces, Buddha statues added to Angkor Wat, and royal dance.

socialStructure.value: Royalty, nobles and officials, Buddhist monks, free farmers and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: A Khmer Buddhist identity linked to the memory of Angkor.

dailyLife.value: Houses on stilts along rivers; rice, fish and fish paste (prahok).

neighbours.value: Ayutthaya and later Siam, the Vietnamese lords and empire, and the Lao kingdoms.

ideasReligions.value: Theravada Buddhist kingship: the king as protector of the faith.

colonisation.value: King Norodom accepted a French protectorate in 1863.

riseSignals.value: Angkor was left around 1431 after a Siamese intervention of unclear nature; capitals: Chaktomuk 1431–1525, Longvek 1525–1594, Srey Sarchor 1594–1620, Oudong 1620–1863.

peakPeriod.value: The page gives no peak for this period; Longvek was the capital from 1525 until Siamese forces took it in 1594.

declineSignals.value: Siam captured Longvek (1594); Vietnam later took the Mekong delta and occupied Cambodia (1834–41).

outcome.value: King Norodom recognised the French protectorate on 11 August 1863.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
